content: Pilot testing should continue until the system design is deemed suitable for nationwide HIV case surveillance. The pilot phase must be structured to provide insights into the human and financial resources necessary for implementing and maintaining the surveillance system. Once the system design is finalized, plans for national implementation should be developed. This rollout can occur in phases or with a single start date. Regardless of the approach, all personnel involved in surveillance activities must undergo training. Technical guidance documents and necessary supplies, such as case report forms, should be distributed. Simple job aids may be helpful in certain settings. Enhanced and frequent monitoring is recommended until the system is well-established and meets performance standards. Continuous training for new facility and surveillance staff will be required, and feedback to these staff members is essential. Data analysis and dissemination should occur as early as possible, accounting for reporting delays and allowing adequate time for complete reporting. Obtaining historical data may pose challenges in some countries. For individuals newly diagnosed with HIV or those experiencing a new sentinel event, case reports will be submitted. However, for individuals with stable HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and without routine viral load monitoring, decisions must be made regarding methods to obtain reports for these cases. Short-term surveillance staff may need to be hired to collect historical case reports. HIV case surveillance data can describe the epidemic in terms of people, place, and time, as well as detect outbreaks or clusters of infection. These data can characterize individuals newly diagnosed with HIV, those with advanced HIV disease or AIDS, and, in settings with reliable mortality data, individuals with HIV who have died. It is important to note that HIV case surveillance captures diagnosed individuals and does not directly measure HIV prevalence or incidence. Surveillance data have been used to mathematically model new HIV infection rates and estimate HIV incidence using special antibody testing methods. Surveillance data must describe sociodemographic characteristics and risk factors to identify transmission modes, geographic disease distribution, and changes over time. These data can be disaggregated to monitor diagnoses among key population groups. However, risk behaviors may change between diagnosis and subsequent sentinel events, potentially leading to overestimates in certain population categories. Surveillance data can strengthen prevention and treatment efforts in areas with high diagnosis rates and identify epidemic concentrations. These data can also be combined with other information, such as program monitoring, qualitative studies, vital statistics, censuses, STI surveillance, and surveys, to account for epidemic changes. Analytical techniques like triangulation, data synthesis, and second-generation surveillance can correlate surveillance data with other sources. HIV case surveillance systems compile care cascade indicators, enabling individual-level analysis while maintaining confidentiality. This provides opportunities to investigate and address gaps in the care cascade. Surveillance data can answer critical questions, such as the annual number of new infections and advanced HIV disease cases, changes over time, affected population groups, and regional distribution of diagnoses. Data analysis must be conducted by staff familiar with the data and its limitations. Analyses should consider how and by whom the data will be used. Assessing stakeholder data needs can guide the types of analyses and presentation formats that facilitate public health action. Surveillance results should ideally be available on the national Ministry of Health website, and data analysis should be automated for future needs. Surveillance programs must ensure data quality, including completeness, timeliness, and accuracy. Incomplete case ascertainment limits data representativeness and utility. Data analysis should account for reporting delays, and caution is necessary when interpreting incomplete variables. Releasing immature surveillance data may lead to misinterpretation. Data must be presented in ways that preserve individual confidentiality to prevent inadvertent identification. Several formats are commonly used to disseminate surveillance data at local, subnational, and national levels. The format should suit the target audience. Data are typically presented in annual HIV surveillance reports, epidemic reports, data fact sheets, and presentations. Annual surveillance reports focus on descriptive statistics and trends in risk patterns, transmission categories, age groups, sex, geographic distribution, and temporal changes. Epidemic reports incorporate broader strategic information, including data on diseases associated with HIV, such as tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections. Data fact sheets provide basic information on specific topics in simple language for general audiences. Presentations and slide sets are useful for disseminating data to government stakeholders, community organizations, donors, and UN agencies. Surveillance data analyses should describe the epidemic by person, place, and time. Outcomes should be disaggregated by demographic and geographic characteristics and examined over time. Demographic variables like age, sex, and race/ethnicity are frequently used for analysis. Gender recording should be carefully considered. Probable transmission routes can serve as proxies for key population groups, enabling data disaggregation. If possible, case characteristics should relate to population denominators to calculate rates. While case counts alone can be informative, variable-specific rates are more useful for risk comparisons. For example, a higher number of cases in one population segment may not indicate a higher rate if that group represents a large proportion of the population. Analysis by place can identify regions with the highest prevalence and new HIV cases. However, the location of reporting may not reflect the place of exposure, particularly for AIDS cases due to the time lag between infection and illness. Comparing place of residence with place of care can highlight service coverage issues. Temporal analysis can reveal trends in disease progression among reported cases. Data should be organized to assess abrupt or gradual changes and compared across time periods. Diagnosis dates, not reporting dates, should be used for trend analysis, and reporting delays must be considered. For example, if the median reporting delay is three months, data for a given year should be analyzed no less than three months after year-end. Descriptive analysis is effective for presenting surveillance data, involving measures of frequency. Basic measures include counts of affected individuals or their characteristics. Case counts can be displayed for populations and variables collected, allowing group comparisons. Percentages and rates are commonly calculated. Percentages represent parts of a total, summing to 100%. Rates are calculated by dividing case numbers by population size for a specified time. Rates based on small numerators (<20) should be noted as unreliable. Standardizing denominators allows direct rate comparisons between populations. Reliable census data are required for rate calculations, typically standardized to 100,000 for national data. Factors influencing data interpretation include population size changes, increased HIV testing coverage, new case definitions, ART initiation guidelines, reporting practices, healthcare facility availability, and duplicate case reports. For example, increased testing may lead to more diagnoses without reflecting epidemic changes. ART provision to individuals with early-stage HIV may slow disease progression, affecting advanced disease trends. Efforts to increase private sector reporting may raise case numbers. User fees may reduce testing uptake, decreasing diagnoses and reports. Duplicate reports may inflate case counts. Surveillance data are generally presented using figures, tables, and maps. Figures and maps display high-level data, while tables provide detailed information. All visualizations should have clear titles, footnotes, and definitions of abbreviations. Figures should include legends, and graph axes should be labeled. Tables should have column and row headings. Examples of published graphs and maps illustrate case surveillance data presentation.
